summary:
Puerto Rico is a United States territory, and the United States federal framework applies on the island in full: federal statutes, executive orders and agency procedure govern entry, documents, screening, federally funded care and federal custody. Puerto Rico's own legislation does not soften that framework, and in the area of trans medical care it sharpens it.

United States travel documents record sex assigned at birth, and Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, eliminated the X marker, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents may present a marker that does not match their appearance at inspection. Entry scrutiny is tightened further for one category of traveller: in February 2025 the United States State Department announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

Airport screening follows federal Transportation Security Administration procedure. All luggage is screened and may be hand-searched; prosthetics, including breast forms, are treated as medically necessary and are not subject to the three-liquid rule, and medical equipment and prosthetics are permitted through the checkpoint after screening. Guidance for trans travellers advises packing strategies that reduce the likelihood of an invasive search. The same procedure applies at Puerto Rico's airports.

In July 2025 Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, barred public funding for it, and set penalties of up to 15 years in prison and a $50,000 fine plus permanent loss of medical licences for doctors who violate the ban. Reporting on the enactment describes a law pushed through non-public hearings and written with deliberate vagueness, so that physicians and affirming parents who facilitate hormone therapy or top surgery risk prosecution, and it requires the education and health departments to run campaigns on the risks of trans-affirming care. The Health Secretary, Ramos Otero, proposed amendments that would have permitted puberty blockers and allowed existing hormone therapy to continue; the enacted text did not adopt them. The report characterises the result as the most extreme care restriction in any United States jurisdiction. The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court, and the outcome of that challenge is not sourced here.

Executive Order 14168 directs federal agencies, including the Bureau of Prisons, to recognise only two sexes, and federal practice has followed by housing transgender inmates according to sex assigned at birth rather than asserted gender identity. The ACLU said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or placed in solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender people in its custody. Advocates argue that the order overrides the Prison Rape Elimination Act requirement that trans inmates' housing be determined by an individual safety assessment. These custody rules govern federal prisoners held in Puerto Rico. No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections trans-inmate housing policy, special unit or judicial ruling was located.

Protection against violence exists on paper and its record of enforcement is thin. Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity, and the territory is also covered by the United States federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. The first hate crime charges in Puerto Rico's history were brought in 2020, after Juan Pagán Bonilla confessed that he and Sean Díaz de León murdered two transgender women on 22 April 2020. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over the ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island.

General non-discrimination coverage stops short of public accommodations. An anti-discrimination bill, House Bill 1725, passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 and would have barred discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in employment, public transportation, public facilities, business transactions and housing, but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved. The 2013 law that did pass, Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013, was amended in the House so that it applies only to employment discrimination, leaving public facilities uncovered.

Conversion therapy for minors remains unregulated in Puerto Rico. The pro-statehood NPP caucus in the Puerto Rico House blocked a floor vote on SB1000 in March 2019, which would have banned the practice for minors despite Senate passage and governor support, with co-sponsor Senator Zoe Laboy dissenting publicly. In April 2019 Governor Alejandro García Padilla announced a pairing of SB1253, framed as clarifying religious freedom principles, with SB1254, a conversion-therapy ban carrying a pastoral exemption for clergy; LGBT council president Johanne Velez García and allies said the pairing would open doors to discrimination by licensing refusal of service on sexual orientation or gender identity grounds. The governor asked lawmakers to withdraw both bills on 13 June 2019 amid sustained opposition. A 2017 religious freedom bill that would have let public businesses legally discriminate against LGBTQ people was vetoed by Governor Ricardo Rosselló in February 2018.

Sexual privacy and relationship recognition were settled through United States federal courts rather than local legislation. Puerto Rico's sodomy ban was upheld by the Puerto Rico Supreme Court in 2002; after Lawrence v. Texas struck down state and territorial sodomy statutes for consensual private acts in 2003, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute. Marriage equality reached the island through federal litigation: four same-sex couples joined the federal lawsuit filed in March 2014, the Ada Conde Vidal case, with Lambda Legal and PR Para Todas intervening, and the plaintiffs included a couple married in Canada in 2007, one married in New York in 2012 and a former National Guard member.

In 2013 the legislature passed House Bill 488, signed 29 May 2013, extending domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Puerto Rico's care ban sits at the restrictive end of United States practice. Reporting on the enactment describes it as the most extreme care restriction among United States jurisdictions, and its scope reaches to age 21 rather than the minors covered by most comparable statutes elsewhere.

Local advocacy has a record of defeating legislation it opposed, which distinguishes the territory's legislative dynamics from its statutory output. The religious-freedom bill pairing was withdrawn in June 2019 after sustained opposition, and a 2017 religious freedom measure was vetoed by the governor in February 2018, yet the 2025 care ban passed despite comparable organisation.

The island's route to legal change has repeatedly run through United States federal courts rather than the local legislature, in sexual privacy in 2003-2004 and in marriage in 2014-2015, so litigation remains a plausible channel for the pending challenge to the care ban.

Reporting on the care ban relies on a single publication's account of the legislative process and its characterisation of the statute; independent verification of the non-public hearings and of the specific drafting choices is not available in the inventory.
localsOnly:
Residents have no statutory ban on conversion therapy for minors. SB1000 died in the House in March 2019, and the 2019 replacement pairing was withdrawn on 13 June 2019, leaving the practice unregulated by local law, subject only to whatever professional discipline applies.

Employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is covered by Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013, but the House amendment confined the statute to employment, so public facilities, transportation, business transactions and housing remain without local protection.

Residents under 21 are barred from gender-affirming care and public funding for it is prohibited, with physicians facing up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine and permanent licence loss. Health and education departments are required to run campaigns on the risks of trans-affirming care, which affects school and clinic environments for young trans residents.

Hate crime charges can be brought under the local 2002 statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity as well as under the United States federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. Domestic violence protections extend to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity under House Bill 488, signed 29 May 2013.

Transgender people held in federal custody are housed according to sex assigned at birth under Executive Order 14168, with no individualised safety assessment required in practice despite the Prison Rape Elimination Act, and the Bureau of Prisons no longer publishes counts of transgender prisoners.
outOfScopeNotes:
No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections policy on trans-inmate housing, dedicated unit or court ruling on the question was located in the sources, so the treatment of trans people in locally run facilities is unresolved rather than known to follow the federal rule.

The litigation announced by the Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation against the July 2025 care ban has no sourced outcome here; whether the ban has been enjoined, amended or is in force unchallenged is unresolved.

Whether the employment-only scope of Senate Bill 238 has since been widened to cover public facilities is not sourced; House Bill 1725's fate after the 2009 Senate inaction is likewise not stated.

The status of conversion therapy regulation after 2019, including any later bill, professional-board rule or executive action, is not sourced beyond the withdrawal recorded in June 2019.

The inventory does not establish how often hate crime charges grounded in gender identity have been brought since 2020, nor whether the January 2021 state of emergency carried funding or task-force machinery; only the declaration itself is sourced.
